raw_json.research_summary: Five independent source verifications were conducted (competency framework revision, blueprint integration, latest regulation and candidate guide, and 90-day cutoff). The synthesis concludes that the 2025 framework was approved (June 19, 2025) and is being phased into exams, with public blueprint integration not conclusively demonstrated as complete as of 2026-09-15. The latest framework in force for exams after Oct 1, 2026 is Essential Competencies for RCIC Practice Version 2026-002. The RCIC EPE Candidate Guide 2026-001 contains the current blueprint details and 90-day cutoff language; the 2021-001 EPE Regulation remains the governing regulation for the EPE, with no 90-day cutoff therein. Key archival items include 2025 June and September board minutes corroborating framework changes and partial alignment.

cf_case_bank.title: The Case of the Misrepresented Work Experience

profile_json.summary: A client, Mr. Singh, seeks assistance from an RCIC to apply for permanent residency in Canada under the Express Entry system. Mr. Singh claims to have five years of work experience as a software engineer, which he believes will enhance his Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score.

timeline_json: January 2023: Mr. Singh contacts the RCIC for an initial consultation.
February 2023: The RCIC submits Mr. Singh's Express Entry profile, including his claimed work experience.
March 2023: Mr. Singh receives an Invitation to Apply (ITA) for permanent residency.
April 2023: During the application process, the RCIC discovers discrepancies in Mr. Singh's employment records.
May 2023: The RCIC confronts Mr. Singh about the discrepancies.
facts_json: Mr. Singh provided letters of reference from his previous employers.
The RCIC noticed inconsistencies in the job titles and durations listed in the reference letters compared to Mr. Singh's resume.
Mr. Singh admitted to exaggerating his work experience to improve his CRS score.
The RCIC is aware that misrepresentation can lead to a five-year ban from entering Canada.

legal: Potential misrepresentation under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
The obligation of the RCIC to report misrepresentation to the immigration authorities.
ethical: The RCIC's duty to maintain honesty and integrity in client representations.
The RCIC's responsibility to advise Mr. Singh of the consequences of misrepresentation.

cf_case_bank.title: The Case of the Cultural Misunderstanding

profile_json.summary: Ms. Chen, a recent immigrant from China, seeks advice from an RCIC regarding her application for a spousal sponsorship. She is sponsoring her husband, who is still residing in China.

timeline_json: March 2023: Ms. Chen submits her spousal sponsorship application with the help of an RCIC.
April 2023: The application is returned due to missing documents.
May 2023: Ms. Chen expresses frustration, citing cultural differences in understanding document requirements.
June 2023: The RCIC arranges a meeting to address Ms. Chen's concerns and clarify the document requirements.
facts_json: Ms. Chen misunderstood the requirement for a police certificate from her husband's country of residence.
The RCIC provided a checklist of required documents, but Ms. Chen found it difficult to understand due to language barriers.
Ms. Chen feels that the RCIC did not adequately explain the importance of each document.

legal: Ensuring compliance with the requirements of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) for spousal sponsorship applications.
ethical: The RCIC's responsibility to ensure clear communication with clients, especially those with language barriers.
The need for cultural competence in advising clients from diverse backgrounds.

cf_case_bank.title: The Case of the Unforeseen Delay

profile_json.summary: Mr. Ahmed, an international student from Egypt, is applying for a Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP) with the assistance of an RCIC. He is concerned about potential delays affecting his ability to work in Canada.

timeline_json: February 2023: Mr. Ahmed completes his studies and becomes eligible for a PGWP.
March 2023: The RCIC submits Mr. Ahmed's PGWP application.
April 2023: Mr. Ahmed receives a job offer contingent upon receiving his PGWP.
May 2023: Processing delays occur due to a backlog at the immigration office.
June 2023: Mr. Ahmed's employer threatens to rescind the job offer if the PGWP is not issued soon.
facts_json: Mr. Ahmed's PGWP application was submitted correctly and on time.
The RCIC informed Mr. Ahmed about potential processing delays at the time of application.
Mr. Ahmed is anxious about losing his job offer due to the delay.

legal: Understanding the implications of processing delays on work permit applications.
Advising clients on their rights and options during unforeseen delays.
ethical: Managing client expectations and providing timely updates on application status.
Balancing client advocacy with realistic outcomes.
